newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-HINGIS LOOKS TO HAVE CLEAR RUN AS SEEDS FALL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HINGIS LOOKS TO HAVE CLEAR RUN AS SEEDS FALL.

text.p: Ill Wimbledon winds have blown away more than half the women's seeds before the fourth round this year, leaving Swiss prodigy Martina Hingis with a practically clear run to the final.
Hingis, the 16-year-old world number one, wobbled during her first round match against Luxembourg qualifier Anne Kremer before coming through 6-4 6-4, but has looked secure since.

She meets 19th-ranked Belgian Sabine Appelmans in Tuesday's fourth round with the prospect of a quarter-final against relative unknowns Denisa Chladkova, an 18-year-old Czech or Venezuelan Maria Alejandra Vento ranked 136 in the world.
The only seeds in her half of the draw are slow-court specialists Irina Spirlea of Romania and Iva Majoli, the woman who beat her in the French open final earlier this month.
The 19-year-old Croatian, who is in fact the only woman to defeat Hingis this year, is likely to prove more of a psychological than competitive barrier.
She has never progressed beyond the first round here before and struggled to win a third round clash with Briton Karen Cross, ranked 320 in the world, 4-6 7-6 6-4.

A more testing opponent might be found in the winner of the duel between two women in form -- Czech Helena Sukova, veteran of 16 Wimbledons and the Russian pretender Anna Kournikova, at 16 years old half her age.

The bottom half of the draw is more crowded. Eighth seed Aranxta Sanchez Vicario, twice runner-up here and ninth seed Mary Pierce must slug it out for a quarter-final place against either Nathalie Tauziat or Sandrine Testud of France.
Sanchez Vicario, who has lost just nine games, the fewest in the draw, in three matches so far, said it was her best start ever at Wimbledon.
"I feel more comfortable with myself now on grass and I've had good preparation," she said.
Testud, ranked 23 in the world, ousted an out-of-sorts second seed Monica Seles 0-6 6-4 8-6 on Monday.
Seles, whose father is ill with cancer, said she could not account for her bad form. She was rattled by a controversial over-ruled call when serving for the match and never recovered.
Testud said top 10 players had to watch out as women's tennis was becoming more competitive.
"Women's tennis has improved a lot. If they don't play really well they can lose and that's what's happening now," the 23-year-old said.
The highest seed left in the bottom half, Jana Novotna, is also the most experienced with a classic serve and volley game well adapted to grass but a fragile psyche.
She is best remembered her for weeping after throwing away a big lead in the 1993 final against Steffi Graf.
Novotna plays 11th seed Mary Joe Fernandez. "That's going to be a tough one," she said.
The pair have met eight times in the last 10 years and they have four victories apiece.
